chapterTitle: SD-WAN Policy Configuration: Centralized Control Policies
aiGenerationNote: Create a 12-minute interactive video tutorial. Use a simulated vManage GUI to walk through the creation of a centralized control policy. First, define site and VPN lists. Then, build an OMP route policy to enforce a hub-and-spoke topology for a specific VPN, showing the `match` (originator site list) and `action` (reject) steps. Next, demonstrate creating a TLOC policy to set preference for "MPLS" over "LTE" colors. Show how to apply the policy to sites and VPNs. Include visual cues highlighting policy flow and impact. End with a hands-on challenge to modify a policy for a different topology.

screens.title: Centralized Control Policies in Cisco SD‑WAN
screens.narratorSegment: We're entering the heart of SD‑WAN intelligence: centralized control policies. These are the policies you build once in vManage and have enforced by vSmart controllers to shape how routes are learned, selected, and shared across the overlay. In practical terms, control policies decide how your network topology behaves — whether branches form a full mesh, are forced to go through a hub, or prefer one transport over another. A concrete example: a hub‑and‑spoke control policy can prevent direct spoke‑to‑spoke learning and force traffic through a data center for inspection. Why this matters: control policies let you express intent centrally, reduce per‑device CLI work, and enforce consistent routing across hundreds of sites. A common misconception is that control policies change packet forwarding directly — they do not; they influence OMP route advertisement and TLOC attributes, which then alter forwarding decisions at the edge. As we proceed, you will learn the building blocks — lists, match conditions, action statements, TLOC policies — and how to apply and verify them. Think of this chapter as the blueprint workshop where you design intent, test it, and confirm it behaves the way you expect.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › Centralized Control Policies
Centralized Control Policies in Cisco SD‑WAN
Define how vSmart evaluates routes and TLOCs to form topology and influence routing decisions across the fabric.
In this lesson
Learn lists, match/action rules, topology and TLOC preference basics, plus verification steps.
Why it matters
Centralized intent reduces errors, enforces security topologies, and supports traffic‑engineering at scale.
Common outcome
Consistent route advertisement and predictable path selection when designed and applied correctly.
Policy Concept Map
Lists → Match → Action → Apply
Topic
Topology control: hub‑and‑spoke vs full mesh
Topic
TLOC preference and traffic engineering
Topic
Apply and verify policies per site and VPN
Explore Key Topics
Three central ideas to carry forward as you build policies.

screens.title: What you'll be able to do
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this lesson you will distinguish centralized control, centralized data, and localized policies; design control policies using lists, match and action rules; craft topology policies like hub‑and‑spoke; create TLOC preference sequences for traffic engineering; and apply and verify policies against specific sites and VPNs. For example, you will be able to create a VPN list for VPN 20, a spoke site list, and a hub site list and then use a route policy to reject spoke originator routes outbound to spokes, enforcing hub transit. This skill matters because it moves routing intent out of device CLI into repeatable, testable policy artifacts managed by vManage and enforced by vSmart. A common misunderstanding is thinking that centralized data policies or localized device templates perform the same role; they control the data plane or device configuration, respectively, not the control plane. As you progress, you will practice designing lists, sequencing rules by specificity, and validating outcomes with vManage and CLI checks. Successful mastery reduces configuration drift, prevents topology leaks, and improves predictable path selection across the overlay.

Mnemonic: Policy as Postal Rules
Think of lists as address books, match conditions as mail filters, and actions as postal rules: accept, reject, or mark priority. This helps you compose complex policies from simple parts.
Example

screens.title: Skills you'll practice
screens.narratorSegment: This lesson will guide hands‑on thinking: define lists, sequence rules, apply direction correctly, and verify outcomes. You will practice creating VPN lists, site lists, and TLOC filters and then using them in OMP route policies and TLOC policies. A practical skill is selecting the correct policy direction: inbound policies affect routes as vSmart receives them from vEdges; outbound policies affect what vSmart advertises back to edges. For instance, enforcing a hub‑and‑spoke topology commonly uses an outbound policy applied from vSmart to spokes to reject routes whose originator is another spoke. Another task is setting TLOC preference values to bias path selection — higher preference values make a TLOC more desirable. We'll also emphasize sequencing: more specific match rules must come before general accept rules to avoid accidental accepts. You'll finish by verifying results with vManage monitoring and edge show commands. Practice in a lab until you can explain why each list and rule exists and what failure would look like. This mental map prevents configuration errors and helps isolate issues during troubleshooting.

keyIdea.title: Practical skills
keyIdea.text: Build lists and correctly order rules; choose inbound vs outbound application; set TLOC preference to steer traffic and verify results.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › Skills to Practice
Core practice steps
  1. Define lists — create VPN, site, and TLOC lists that express intent for rules.
  2. Compose rules — sequence match conditions and action statements, more specific first.
  3. Apply correctly — choose inbound or outbound depending on whether you alter input to vSmart or what vSmart advertises.
  4. Verify — use vManage and edge show commands to confirm routes and TLOC attributes.
VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE
Mnemonic: Sequence matters
Always place restrictive rejects or specific site matches before broad accepts. If a specific deny is placed after a general accept, it will never run.
Example
Apply an outbound OMP route policy to spokes rejecting originator spoke routes to enforce hub transit.
Check
After apply, confirm spokes do not learn direct OMP routes from other spokes with show omp routes.

screens.title: Policy Categories: Control, Data, Localized
screens.narratorSegment: Start by anchoring the three policy categories and what each controls. A centralized control policy is configured in vManage and enforced by vSmart; it influences the control plane — how routes are advertised and which paths are known across the overlay. Centralized data policies also live in vManage but they operate on the data plane: they steer packets at the edge, apply application awareness, QoS, or firewall actions. Localized policies are device‑level configurations applied directly on vEdge or cEdge devices (or via device templates) for interface settings, local QoS, or access lists. A concrete example: to prevent direct spoke-to-spoke routing, you use a centralized control policy because it changes which OMP routes are advertised. If your goal is to mark packets for QoS or block an application at the branch, you would use a centralized data policy. A common misconception is to assume centralized control policies immediately change forwarding at the edge; instead they change route advertisement and attributes like preference or weight that indirectly alter forwarding. Key takeaway: choose the policy category that targets the plane and outcome you need — control for route advertisement and topology, data for forwarding behavior, localized for device specifics.

keyIdea.title: Three policy planes
keyIdea.text: Control affects routing and topology via vSmart; Data affects forwarding on edges; Localized affects device-specific settings.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › Policy Categories
Policy Categories
Understand the plane each policy affects and a practical example for when to use it.
Centralized Control
vManage → vSmart. Controls route advertisement, topology, and TLOC attributes. Example: enforce hub‑and‑spoke.
Centralized Data
vManage → vSmart for data enforcement. Controls QoS, application steering, firewall behavior at the edge.
Localized Policies
Device templates and direct device config: interface settings, local QoS, access lists.
Concrete contrast
To stop branch A from talking directly to branch B, use control policies. To drop an application flow at branch A, use a data policy.
Misconception check
Control policies do not directly alter packet headers; they change what routes and TLOC attributes vSmart advertises, which affects forwarding decisions.
Quick Example
Enforce hub transit for VPN 20 by rejecting OMP routes whose originator is a spoke when advertising to spokes.
Key Takeaway

Pick the policy type that matches the plane you need to control: routing, forwarding, or device configuration.

screens.title: How vSmart Applies Control Policies via OMP
screens.narratorSegment: Control policies are implemented as structured artifacts in vManage and enforced by vSmart via OMP. At the heart of each policy are lists — VPN lists, site lists, prefix lists, and TLOC lists — which become reusable match criteria. Policies are composed as ordered sequences of rules. Each rule has match conditions and an action statement, such as accept, reject, or set preference. vSmart evaluates inbound policies when it receives routes from vEdge/cEdge devices and evaluates outbound policies when advertising routes back to edges. For example, you might create a VPN list containing VPN 10, a site list with spoke site IDs, and then build an OMP route policy sequence that rejects routes originating from spokes when advertising to spokes. The policy does not immediately change packet forwarding; it changes which OMP routes are advertised and the TLOC attributes carried with those routes. Practically, this means the edge devices will only learn routes and TLOC preferences that vSmart allows, which then influence the next‑hop selection and forwarding. A common mistake is applying the wrong direction — an inbound policy to spokes will not stop vSmart advertising spoke originator routes to other spokes; an outbound policy is required. Always test policy direction with a small site group before broad deployment.

keyIdea.title: Policy enforcement path
keyIdea.text: vManage builds the policy; vSmart evaluates it and uses OMP to control which routes and TLOC attributes are advertised to edges.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › vSmart & OMP
Policy Construction Flow
Reusable lists feed rule sequences which vSmart evaluates to control OMP advertisements.
Step 1: Define lists
VPN lists, site lists, prefix lists, and TLOC lists are created as reusable building blocks.
Step 2: Compose rule sequences
Each rule has match conditions and an action. Order matters: specific rejects before general accepts.
Step 3: Apply with direction
Choose inbound or outbound to control how vSmart receives or advertises routes from edges.
Annotated Example
Imagine a policy that rejects spokes' originator routes when advertising to spokes. When vSmart applies this outbound policy, spokes will no longer receive direct spoke routes and will send traffic via the hub.
# Conceptual OMP Route Policy (excerpt)
Sequence 10:
  Match:
    Route Type: OMP
    Originator Site List: Spoke_Sites
  Action:
    Reject
Sequence 20:
  Match:
    VPN List: VPN_20_Only
  Action:
    Accept
Key Takeaway

Control policies act by changing the set of advertised OMP routes and their attributes, not by directly manipulating packet headers.

screens.title: Topology Options: Full‑Mesh vs Hub‑and‑Spoke
screens.narratorSegment: SD‑WAN natively supports a full‑mesh overlay, where sites can learn each other's routes and connect directly. That topology is optimal for minimizing hop count and avoiding central bottlenecks. However, many organizations intentionally implement a hub‑and‑spoke topology for security, centralized services, or compliance. In a hub‑and‑spoke design, spoke sites should not learn direct OMP routes from other spokes; instead, spokes learn remote routes via the hub. Control policies implement this by rejecting OMP routes originating from spokes when advertising to spokes or by manipulating TLOC visibility. A concrete example: in VPN 10, you create a VPN list for VPN 10, a site list for spokes 201–203, and an outbound OMP route policy that rejects originator routes from Spoke_Sites. The hub accepts and redistributes spoke routes. A common misconception is that hub‑and‑spoke means disabling direct data paths at the transport layer — it doesn’t. It prevents route advertisement so that traffic is forced to traverse the hub by route visibility. Consider latency and bandwidth tradeoffs; forcing all branch traffic through a hub can add latency and create a bottleneck, so apply this topology only when the security or service requirements justify it.

keyIdea.title: Topology tradeoffs
keyIdea.text: Full mesh minimizes path length; hub‑and‑spoke centralizes services but may increase latency and load at the hub. Control policies enforce which topology is learned.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › Topology Choices
Full‑Mesh
All sites learn each other's routes. Benefits: direct paths, lower latency. Use when branches need peer connectivity and bandwidth is available.
When to use
Distributed applications, peer services, and low latency requirements.
Tradeoffs
More direct paths but less central control for inspection or legacy services.
Hub‑and‑Spoke
Spokes only learn remote routes via the hub. Benefits: central inspection, simplified security. Use when traffic must be inspected or passes through centralized services.
How to implement
Create OMP route policy that rejects spoke originator routes when advertising to spokes; allow hub to accept and redistribute.
Warning
Forcing hub transit can create latency and central bottlenecks; test capacity and latency before wide rollout.
Concrete Scenario
Enforce hub transit for VPN 20 so branches 201–203 cannot directly learn each other's routes; all inter‑branch traffic must go through Site 100 for inspection.

screens.title: Hub‑and‑Spoke Control Policy Example
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a conceptual hub‑and‑spoke control policy and what each section does. First, define three lists: a VPN list that contains the VPN you wish to restrict, a spoke site list containing your branch site IDs, and a hub site list for the data center. These lists make match conditions readable and reusable. In the policy body, define an OMP route policy with a sequence that matches routes whose originator belongs to Spoke_Sites and whose VPN is the target; the action for that sequence is reject, preventing vSmart from advertising those routes to spokes. Follow this with a more general accept sequence for the VPN so hub originator routes and other necessary routes are still advertised. A concrete example: apply this policy outbound from vSmart to the spokes; when vSmart evaluates advertising to a spoke, it will hit the reject sequence for routes that originate at other spokes and not advertise them. A common error is applying the policy inbound to spokes; inbound affects routes as vSmart receives them, not what it advertises back. Always test with one spoke pair first and confirm with show omp routes and show policy from-vsmart.

keyIdea.title: Reject originator rule
keyIdea.text: Rejecting routes whose originator is another spoke stops direct spoke‑to‑spoke learning and enforces hub transit.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › Hub & Spoke Example
Lists and Policy Structure
Create reusable lists and an ordered OMP route policy with specific reject rules before accept rules.
VPN List
VPN_20_Only contains VPN 20.
Site Lists
Spoke_Sites: 201,202,203. Hub_Sites: 100.
Conceptual Policy Snippet
# Policy Name: Hub_Spoke_VPN20
# Applied Outbound from vSmart to Spoke_Sites
OMP Route Policy:
  Sequence 10:
    Match:
      VPN List: VPN_20_Only
      Originator Site List: Spoke_Sites
    Action:
      Reject
  Sequence 20:
    Match:
      VPN List: VPN_20_Only
    Action:
      Accept
Apply outbound to spokes so vSmart does not advertise routes that originate at other spokes. Test with a single spoke pair first.
Common Mistake

Applying the policy in the wrong direction or placing accept before reject will fail to enforce hub transit. Sequence and application direction are critical.

screens.title: TLOC: What it is and why it matters
screens.narratorSegment: A TLOC, or transport locator, is the identifier vSmart uses to reference a specific WAN interface on an edge device. It is a tuple composed of system IP, color, and encapsulation — together they describe where a route came from and the transport it uses. Understanding TLOCs is essential for traffic engineering because control policies can change TLOC attributes such as preference or weight. A practical example: you might have two TLOCs at a site — one colored mpls and one colored lte. By setting a higher TLOC preference for mpls in your control policy for VPN 10, you cause vSmart to advertise routes with the MPLS TLOC as preferred, prompting edges to select MPLS even if LTE occasionally has lower latency. A misconception is to treat colors as mere labels; they are policy primitives used in match conditions and TLOC sequences. When you create a TLOC policy sequence, you should explicitly match TLOC color and VPN or site lists, then set preference values. This explicit control gives you consistent transport bias across the fabric and helps meet performance, cost, and security objectives.

keyIdea.title: TLOC basics
keyIdea.text: TLOC = system IP + color + encapsulation. Policies can set TLOC preference or weight to steer path selection.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › TLOCs
What is a TLOC?
A TLOC identifies a transport interface by system IP, color, and encapsulation type. It’s used in route advertisement and match conditions.
Example
Site A has TLOC mpls (system IP 10.0.0.1) and TLOC lte (system IP 10.0.0.2). Policy sets preference to favor mpls for critical VPNs.
Match primitives
You can match TLOC Color, Site ID, or VPN and then set preference, weight, or exclude TLOCs from advertisement.
TLOC Preference Example
# Prefer MPLS for VPN 10
Sequence 10:
  Match:
    TLOC Color: mpls
    VPN List: VPN_10_List
  Action:
    Set TLOC Preference: 500
Sequence 20:
  Match:
    TLOC Color: biz-internet
    VPN List: VPN_10_List
  Action:
    Set TLOC Preference: 100
Setting higher preference values biases vSmart’s choice of TLOC when advertising routes to edges, guiding the edge forwarding selection.

screens.title: Designing a TLOC Preference Policy
screens.narratorSegment: Designing a TLOC preference policy is a practical traffic engineering step. Begin by defining the VPN or site lists that scope your change. Next, create a TLOC policy with ordered sequences: first match the preferred TLOC color and set a higher preference; next match the less desired color and set a lower preference. For example, when you want MPLS prioritized for VPN 10, the first sequence matches TLOC Color: mpls and the VPN list and sets preference to 500. The second sequence matches biz‑internet and sets preference to 100. Apply this control policy inbound to vSmart from the edges so vSmart stores those TLOC preferences when it processes incoming routes. Why apply inbound? Because you want vSmart to record the adjusted TLOC attributes as it learns them. A typical misconception is to set preferences only on the edge devices; centralized control policies allow consistent, fabric‑wide preference values. After applying, verify with show omp tlocs and show omp routes to confirm the advertised preference values. If you see unexpected selection, check for policy order, whether the VPN list scopes the change correctly, and that the policy application direction is inbound.

keyIdea.title: TLOC policy recipe
keyIdea.text: Define scope lists, sequence matches by preference order, apply inbound to vSmart, and verify with OMP show commands.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › TLOC Preference Workflow
Step-by-step
  1. 1. Define lists — VPN_10_List or All_Sites depending on scope.
  2. 2. Create TLOC sequences — match color mpls, set high preference; match other colors, set low preference.
  3. 3. Apply inbound — applied inbound to vSmart so it learns TLOC attributes with the new preference.
  4. 4. Verify — check show omp tlocs and show omp routes; confirm advertised preference values.
Example snippet
# Prefer MPLS for VPN 10
Sequence 10:
  Match:
    TLOC Color: mpls
    VPN List: VPN_10_List
  Action:
    Set TLOC Preference: 500
Sequence 20:
  Match:
    TLOC Color: biz-internet
    VPN List: VPN_10_List
  Action:
    Set TLOC Preference: 100
If the policy has no effect, verify the VPN and site lists contain the expected members and that the policy is applied inbound to vSmart from the relevant sites.

screens.title: Applying Policies: Scope and Direction
screens.narratorSegment: Applying a control policy requires careful scoping and direction selection. Scope is defined by the VPN List and Site List you pass into the policy application. Direction determines whether the policy is evaluated as vSmart receives routes (inbound) or as vSmart advertises routes back to edges (outbound). A practical rule: use inbound when you want to modify attributes or TLOC preference as vSmart learns them, and use outbound when you want to control what routes are advertised to a target set of edges, such as preventing spokes from receiving other spoke originator routes. For example, to stop spokes learning other spokes' routes, apply the hub‑and‑spoke OMP route policy outbound with From: Spoke_Sites and To: VPN_20_Only. Misapplying direction is a common cause of policies not producing the expected effect. Always document the From/To scope and test with a single site pair. After application, use vManage Monitor to see control connections and on edges run show omp routes and show omp tlocs to confirm whether routes and TLOC attributes reflect the policy. If results are unexpected, recheck list membership, rule sequence, and application direction as a first troubleshooting step.

narration.text: Applying a control policy requires careful scoping and direction selection. Scope is defined by the VPN List and Site List you pass into the policy application. Direction determines whether the policy is evaluated as vSmart receives routes (inbound) or as vSmart advertises routes back to edges (outbound). A practical rule: use inbound when you want to modify attributes or TLOC preference as vSmart learns them, and use outbound when you want to control what routes are advertised to a target set of edges, such as preventing spokes from receiving other spoke originator routes. For example, to stop spokes learning other spokes' routes, apply the hub‑and‑spoke OMP route policy outbound with From: Spoke_Sites and To: VPN_20_Only. Misapplying direction is a common cause of policies not producing the expected effect. Always document the From/To scope and test with a single site pair. After application, use vManage Monitor to see control connections and on edges run show omp routes and show omp tlocs to confirm whether routes and TLOC attributes reflect the policy. If results are unexpected, recheck list membership, rule sequence, and application direction as a first troubleshooting step.

Define which sites and VPNs the policy affects and whether it is inbound or outbound relative to vSmart.
From
The site(s) or site list that are the source for the policy application.
To

screens.title: Best Practices and Common Mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: Designing safe, effective control policies requires following best practices and watching for common mistakes. First, always assume 'accept' is the default when no rule matches; explicitly reject when you need to prevent a route. Second, sequence rules from specific to general — a specific reject must appear before a broad accept to take effect. Third, test changes in a lab or with a small group of sites before rolling out to production. Fourth, document the From/To scope and the intended effect so future engineers can audit policy intent. Common mistakes include applying the policy in the wrong direction, forgetting to include the correct site or VPN in the lists, placing accept rules before rejects, and altering TLOC preference values without checking for service‑impact tradeoffs. A concrete example: if spokes can still talk directly after applying a hub‑and‑spoke policy, likely the action for the spoke‑originator rule is accept or the policy was applied inbound instead of outbound. Finally, always verify after application: check vManage control connections and run show omp routes and show omp tlocs on edges. These steps prevent black holes, loops, and unintended path selection.

screens.title: Verify Policy Impact
screens.narratorSegment: Verification confirms that your intended policy behavior appears in the control plane and is reflected at the edge. fullNarratorScript:
We're entering the heart of SD‑WAN intelligence: centralized control policies. These are the policies you build once in vManage and have enforced by vSmart controllers to shape how routes are learned, selected, and shared across the overlay. In practical terms, control policies decide how your network topology behaves — whether branches form a full mesh, are forced to go through a hub, or prefer one transport over another. A concrete example: a hub‑and‑spoke control policy can prevent direct spoke‑to‑spoke learning and force traffic through a data center for inspection. Why this matters: control policies let you express intent centrally, reduce per‑device CLI work, and enforce consistent routing across hundreds of sites. A common misconception is that control policies change packet forwarding directly — they do not; they influence OMP route advertisement and TLOC attributes, which then alter forwarding decisions at the edge. As we proceed, you will learn the building blocks — lists, match conditions, action statements, TLOC policies — and how to apply and verify them. Think of this chapter as the blueprint workshop where you design intent, test it, and confirm it behaves the way you expect.

By the end of this lesson you will distinguish centralized control, centralized data, and localized policies; design control policies using lists, match and action rules; craft topology policies like hub‑and‑spoke; create TLOC preference sequences for traffic engineering; and apply and verify policies against specific sites and VPNs. For example, you will be able to create a VPN list for VPN 20, a spoke site list, and a hub site list and then use a route policy to reject spoke originator routes outbound to spokes, enforcing hub transit. This skill matters because it moves routing intent out of device CLI into repeatable, testable policy artifacts managed by vManage and enforced by vSmart. A common misunderstanding is thinking that centralized data policies or localized device templates perform the same role; they control the data plane or device configuration, respectively, not the control plane. As you progress, you will practice designing lists, sequencing rules by specificity, and validating outcomes with vManage and CLI checks. Successful mastery reduces configuration drift, prevents topology leaks, and improves predictable path selection across the overlay.

This lesson will guide hands‑on thinking: define lists, sequence rules, apply direction correctly, and verify outcomes. You will practice creating VPN lists, site lists, and TLOC filters and then using them in OMP route policies and TLOC policies. A practical skill is selecting the correct policy direction: inbound policies affect routes as vSmart receives them from vEdges; outbound policies affect what vSmart advertises back to edges. For instance, enforcing a hub‑and‑spoke topology commonly uses an outbound policy applied from vSmart to spokes to reject routes whose originator is another spoke. Another task is setting TLOC preference values to bias path selection — higher preference values make a TLOC more desirable. We'll also emphasize sequencing: more specific match rules must come before general accept rules to avoid accidental accepts. You'll finish by verifying results with vManage monitoring and edge show commands. Practice in a lab until you can explain why each list and rule exists and what failure would look like. This mental map prevents configuration errors and helps isolate issues during troubleshooting.

Start by anchoring the three policy categories and what each controls. A centralized control policy is configured in vManage and enforced by vSmart; it influences the control plane — how routes are advertised and which paths are known across the overlay. Centralized data policies also live in vManage but they operate on the data plane: they steer packets at the edge, apply application awareness, QoS, or firewall actions. Localized policies are device‑level configurations applied directly on vEdge or cEdge devices (or via device templates) for interface settings, local QoS, or access lists. A concrete example: to prevent direct spoke-to-spoke routing, you use a centralized control policy because it changes which OMP routes are advertised. If your goal is to mark packets for QoS or block an application at the branch, you would use a centralized data policy. A common misconception is to assume centralized control policies immediately change forwarding at the edge; instead they change route advertisement and attributes like preference or weight that indirectly alter forwarding. Key takeaway: choose the policy category that targets the plane and outcome you need — control for route advertisement and topology, data for forwarding behavior, localized for device specifics.

Control policies are implemented as structured artifacts in vManage and enforced by vSmart via OMP. At the heart of each policy are lists — VPN lists, site lists, prefix lists, and TLOC lists — which become reusable match criteria. Policies are composed as ordered sequences of rules. Each rule has match conditions and an action statement, such as accept, reject, or set preference. vSmart evaluates inbound policies when it receives routes from vEdge/cEdge devices and evaluates outbound policies when advertising routes back to edges. For example, you might create a VPN list containing VPN 10, a site list with spoke site IDs, and then build an OMP route policy sequence that rejects routes originating from spokes when advertising to spokes. The policy does not immediately change packet forwarding; it changes which OMP routes are advertised and the TLOC attributes carried with those routes. Practically, this means the edge devices will only learn routes and TLOC preferences that vSmart allows, which then influence the next‑hop selection and forwarding. A common mistake is applying the wrong direction — an inbound policy to spokes will not stop vSmart advertising spoke originator routes to other spokes; an outbound policy is required. Always test policy direction with a small site group before broad deployment.

SD‑WAN natively supports a full‑mesh overlay, where sites can learn each other's routes and connect directly. That topology is optimal for minimizing hop count and avoiding central bottlenecks. However, many organizations intentionally implement a hub‑and‑spoke topology for security, centralized services, or compliance. In a hub‑and‑spoke design, spoke sites should not learn direct OMP routes from other spokes; instead, spokes learn remote routes via the hub. Control policies implement this by rejecting OMP routes originating from spokes when advertising to spokes or by manipulating TLOC visibility. A concrete example: in VPN 10, you create a VPN list for VPN 10, a site list for spokes 201–203, and an outbound OMP route policy that rejects originator routes from Spoke_Sites. The hub accepts and redistributes spoke routes. A common misconception is that hub‑and‑spoke means disabling direct data paths at the transport layer — it doesn’t. It prevents route advertisement so that traffic is forced to traverse the hub by route visibility. Consider latency and bandwidth tradeoffs; forcing all branch traffic through a hub can add latency and create a bottleneck, so apply this topology only when the security or service requirements justify it.

Let's walk through a conceptual hub‑and‑spoke control policy and what each section does. First, define three lists: a VPN list that contains the VPN you wish to restrict, a spoke site list containing your branch site IDs, and a hub site list for the data center. These lists make match conditions readable and reusable. In the policy body, define an OMP route policy with a sequence that matches routes whose originator belongs to Spoke_Sites and whose VPN is the target; the action for that sequence is reject, preventing vSmart from advertising those routes to spokes. Follow this with a more general accept sequence for the VPN so hub originator routes and other necessary routes are still advertised. A concrete example: apply this policy outbound from vSmart to the spokes; when vSmart evaluates advertising to a spoke, it will hit the reject sequence for routes that originate at other spokes and not advertise them. A common error is applying the policy inbound to spokes; inbound affects routes as vSmart receives them, not what it advertises back. Always test with one spoke pair first and confirm with show omp routes and show policy from-vsmart.

A TLOC, or transport locator, is the identifier vSmart uses to reference a specific WAN interface on an edge device. It is a tuple composed of system IP, color, and encapsulation — together they describe where a route came from and the transport it uses. Understanding TLOCs is essential for traffic engineering because control policies can change TLOC attributes such as preference or weight. A practical example: you might have two TLOCs at a site — one colored mpls and one colored lte. By setting a higher TLOC preference for mpls in your control policy for VPN 10, you cause vSmart to advertise routes with the MPLS TLOC as preferred, prompting edges to select MPLS even if LTE occasionally has lower latency. A misconception is to treat colors as mere labels; they are policy primitives used in match conditions and TLOC sequences. When you create a TLOC policy sequence, you should explicitly match TLOC color and VPN or site lists, then set preference values. This explicit control gives you consistent transport bias across the fabric and helps meet performance, cost, and security objectives.

Designing a TLOC preference policy is a practical traffic engineering step. Begin by defining the VPN or site lists that scope your change. Next, create a TLOC policy with ordered sequences: first match the preferred TLOC color and set a higher preference; next match the less desired color and set a lower preference. For example, when you want MPLS prioritized for VPN 10, the first sequence matches TLOC Color: mpls and the VPN list and sets preference to 500. The second sequence matches biz‑internet and sets preference to 100. Apply this control policy inbound to vSmart from the edges so vSmart stores those TLOC preferences when it processes incoming routes. Why apply inbound? Because you want vSmart to record the adjusted TLOC attributes as it learns them. A typical misconception is to set preferences only on the edge devices; centralized control policies allow consistent, fabric‑wide preference values. After applying, verify with show omp tlocs and show omp routes to confirm the advertised preference values. If you see unexpected selection, check for policy order, whether the VPN list scopes the change correctly, and that the policy application direction is inbound.
